1. Core Foundations: Mathematical Operators & Digit Processing Pattern

Basic Mathematics DSA ka sabse fundamental building block hai. Competitive programming aur interview problems me lagbhag har numerical problem Modulo (%) aur Integer Division (/) ke combination par depend karti hai.

Operator Mathematical Meaning Execution Example DSA Application
% (Modulo) Division ke baad ka Remainder deta hai 123 % 10 = 3 Rightmost (last) digit ko extract karna
/ (Division) Integer division (fractional part discard) 123 / 10 = 12 Rightmost (last) digit ko eliminate/hata dena
== (Equality) Check karta hai ki left aur right values equal hain original == rev Palindrome aur Armstrong conditions verify karna
!= (Not Equal) Check karta hai values unequal hain digit % 2 != 0 Odd digits aur termination check (b != 0)
Universal Digit Processing Idiom:

Kisi bhi positive integer n ke digits ko right-to-left process karne ke liye standard loop template: 

while (n > 0) {
    int digit = n % 10;
    n = n / 10;
}

2. The 13 Core Math Problems: Brute, Better & Optimal Solutions

Problem 1

Count All Digits of a Number

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given an integer n, count and return the total number of digits.

Example 1:
Input: n = 12345
Output: 5
Explanation: 12345 has 5 distinct digits.
Example 2:
Input: n = 7
Output: 1
Explanation: Single digit number.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Maths Formula: Kisi number $N$ ke digits ki count $\lfloor \log_{10}(N) \rfloor + 1$ hoti hai! Loop chalane ke bajaye single math operation $O(1)$ time me solve kar deta hai.
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: n = 7789
log10(7789) = 3.89148
floor(3.89148) = 3
count = 3 + 1 = 4 digits.
Answer: 4
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Convert number to string using to_string(n) and return string length.
Time: O(log10 N) • Space: O(log10 N)
🟡 Better Approach:
Iterative division: while (n > 0) { count++; n /= 10; }
Time: O(log10 N) • Space: O(1)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Logarithmic formula: int(log10(n) + 1). O(1) time and space.
Time: O(1) • Space: O(1)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

int countDigitsBrute(int n) {
    string s = to_string(abs(n));
    return s.length();
}

int main() {
    cout << countDigitsBrute(12345) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int countDigitsBetter(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 1;
    n = abs(n);
    int count = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        count++;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return count;
}

int main() {
    cout << countDigitsBetter(12345) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <cmath>
using namespace std;

int countDigitsOptimal(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 1;
    return (int)log10(abs(n)) + 1;
}

int main() {
    cout << countDigitsOptimal(12345) << endl;
    return 0;
}
Problem 2

Count Number of Odd Digits in a Number

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given an integer n, count and return the number of digits that are odd.

Example 1:
Input: n = 12345
Output: 3
Explanation: Digits 1, 3, and 5 are odd.
Example 2:
Input: n = 2468
Output: 0
Explanation: All digits are even.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Number ko `% 10` karke aakhiri digit extract karo, bitwise check `(digit & 1)` se odd verify karo, aur number ko `/ 10` se reduce karte jao.
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: n = 1352
2 → Even, skip
5 → Odd, count = 1
3 → Odd, count = 2
1 → Odd, count = 3. Result = 3.
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Convert to string, check if (char - '0') % 2 != 0 for each character.
Time: O(log10 N) • Space: O(log10 N)
🟡 Better Approach:
Recursion: return (n % 2 != 0) + countOdd(n / 10).
Time: O(log10 N) • Space: O(log10 N) stack
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Iterative bitwise modulo: while (n > 0) { if ((n % 10) & 1) count++; n /= 10; } O(1) space.
Time: O(log10 N) • Space: O(1)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

int countOddDigitsBrute(int n) {
    string s = to_string(abs(n));
    int count = 0;
    for (char c : s) {
        if ((c - '0') % 2 != 0) count++;
    }
    return count;
}

int main() {
    cout << countOddDigitsBrute(1234567) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int countOddDigitsBetter(int n) {
    n = abs(n);
    int count = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        int d = n % 10;
        if (d % 2 != 0) count++;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return count;
}

int main() {
    cout << countOddDigitsBetter(1234567) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int countOddDigitsOptimal(int n) {
    n = abs(n);
    int count = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        count += ((n % 10) & 1);
        n /= 10;
    }
    return count;
}

int main() {
    cout << countOddDigitsOptimal(1234567) << endl;
    return 0;
}
Problem 3

Reverse a Number

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given a signed 32-bit integer n, return n with its digits reversed, with 32-bit overflow check.

Example 1:
Input: n = 123
Output: 321
Explanation: Digits inverted in place.
Example 2:
Input: n = -120
Output: -21
Explanation: Negative sign preserved and trailing zero eliminated.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Base-10 shifting: `rev = rev * 10 + (n % 10)`. Multiplication se pehle overflow check: `if (rev > INT_MAX / 10 || rev < INT_MIN / 10) return 0`.
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: n = 123
d = 3: rev = 0 * 10 + 3 = 3
d = 2: rev = 3 * 10 + 2 = 32
d = 1: rev = 32 * 10 + 1 = 321. Result = 321.
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Convert to string, reverse using std::reverse, parse back with stoll and clamp.
Time: O(log10 N) • Space: O(log10 N)
🟡 Better Approach:
Accumulate reversed digits using 64-bit integer (long long) and clamp to 32-bit limits.
Time: O(log10 N) • Space: O(1)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Pure 32-bit arithmetic with proactive boundary checking: if (rev > INT_MAX / 10) return 0.
Time: O(log10 N) • Space: O(1)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

long long reverseNumberBrute(int n) {
    bool neg = n < 0;
    string s = to_string(abs(n));
    reverse(s.begin(), s.end());
    long long rev = stoll(s);
    return neg ? -rev : rev;
}

int main() {
    cout << reverseNumberBrute(1234) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

long long reverseNumberBetter(int n) {
    long long rev = 0;
    bool neg = n < 0;
    n = abs(n);
    while (n > 0) {
        rev = rev * 10 + (n % 10);
        n /= 10;
    }
    return neg ? -rev : rev;
}

int main() {
    cout << reverseNumberBetter(1234) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <climits>
using namespace std;

int reverseNumberOptimal(int x) {
    int rev = 0;
    while (x != 0) {
        int pop = x % 10;
        x /= 10;
        if (rev > INT_MAX / 10 || (rev == INT_MAX / 10 && pop > 7)) return 0;
        if (rev < INT_MIN / 10 || (rev == INT_MIN / 10 && pop < -8)) return 0;
        rev = rev * 10 + pop;
    }
    return rev;
}

int main() {
    cout << reverseNumberOptimal(1234) << endl;
    return 0;
}
Problem 4

Palindrome Number

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given an integer n, return true if n is a palindrome integer, and false otherwise.

Example 1:
Input: n = 121
Output: true
Explanation: 121 reads 121 from left to right and from right to left.
Example 2:
Input: n = -121
Output: false
Explanation: From left to right it reads -121. From right to left it becomes 121-.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Negative numbers kbhi palindrome nahi ho sakte. Half-reversal optimization: sirf aadhi string/number ko reverse karo jab tak `rev < n`. Agar `n == rev || n == rev / 10`, to palindrome hai!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: n = 1221
Step 1: rev = 1, n = 122
Step 2: rev = 12, n = 12
Now n == rev (12 == 12) → Even palindrome match! Return true.
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Convert integer to string and check if string equals its reverse.
Time: O(log10 N) • Space: O(log10 N)
🟡 Better Approach:
Fully reverse integer using modulo arithmetic and compare reversed == original.
Time: O(log10 N) • Space: O(1)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Revert half of the number: while (n > rev) { rev = rev * 10 + n % 10; n /= 10; }. Check n == rev || n == rev / 10.
Time: O(log10(N) / 2) • Space: O(1)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

bool isPalindromeBrute(int n) {
    if (n < 0) return false;
    string s = to_string(n);
    string r = s;
    reverse(r.begin(), r.end());
    return s == r;
}

int main() {
    cout << (isPalindromeBrute(121) ? "true" : "false") << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

bool isPalindromeBetter(int n) {
    if (n < 0) return false;
    long long rev = 0;
    int temp = n;
    while (temp > 0) {
        rev = rev * 10 + (temp % 10);
        temp /= 10;
    }
    return rev == n;
}

int main() {
    cout << (isPalindromeBetter(121) ? "true" : "false") << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

bool isPalindromeOptimal(int x) {
    if (x < 0 || (x % 10 == 0 && x != 0)) return false;
    int reverted = 0;
    while (x > reverted) {
        reverted = reverted * 10 + (x % 10);
        x /= 10;
    }
    return x == reverted || x == reverted / 10;
}

int main() {
    cout << (isPalindromeOptimal(121) ? "true" : "false") << endl;
    return 0;
}
Problem 5

Largest Digit in a Number

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given an integer n, find and return the largest digit present in the number.

Example 1:
Input: n = 28549
Output: 9
Explanation: The maximum digit in 28549 is 9.
Example 2:
Input: n = 4
Output: 4
Explanation: Single digit is the largest.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Modulo loop: `maxD = max(maxD, n % 10)`. Early Exit: Agar kisi point par `maxD == 9` mil jaye, to loop break kar do kyunki 9 se bada decimal digit ho hi nahi sakta!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: n = 285
5 → maxD = 5, n = 28
8 → maxD = 8, n = 2
2 → 2 < 8 → maxD = 8. Output = 8.
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Convert to string, sort characters descending, return first character.
Time: O(K log K) • Space: O(K)
🟡 Better Approach:
Full division scan updating maxDigit = max(maxDigit, n % 10).
Time: O(log10 N) • Space: O(1)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Division scan with early termination: if (maxD == 9) break; O(1) space.
Time: O(log10 N) • Space: O(1)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int largestDigitBrute(int n) {
    string s = to_string(abs(n));
    sort(s.begin(), s.end());
    return s.back() - '0';
}

int main() {
    cout << largestDigitBrute(29461) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int largestDigitBetter(int n) {
    n = abs(n);
    int maxD = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        maxD = max(maxD, n % 10);
        n /= 10;
    }
    return maxD;
}

int main() {
    cout << largestDigitBetter(29461) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int largestDigitOptimal(int n) {
    n = abs(n);
    int maxD = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        int d = n % 10;
        if (d > maxD) maxD = d;
        if (maxD == 9) break;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return maxD;
}

int main() {
    cout << largestDigitOptimal(29461) << endl;
    return 0;
}
Problem 6

Factorial of a Given Number

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given an integer n, calculate and return its factorial $n!$.

Example 1:
Input: n = 5
Output: 120
Explanation: 5! = 5 * 4 * 3 * 2 * 1 = 120.
Example 2:
Input: n = 0
Output: 1
Explanation: 0! is defined as 1.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Accumulate multiplication: `ans = 1; for (i = 1 to n) ans *= i;`. 64-bit unsigned integer `long long` use karo taaki $N \le 20$ tak overflow na ho.
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: n = 4
1 * 1 = 1
1 * 2 = 2
2 * 3 = 6
6 * 4 = 24. Result = 24.
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Recursive factorial definition: return n * fact(n - 1).
Time: O(N) • Space: O(N) stack
🟡 Better Approach:
Dynamic programming table dp[n + 1] storing intermediate factorials.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(N)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Iterative 64-bit loop: ans = 1; for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) ans *= i; O(1) space.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(1)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

long long factorialBrute(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1;

}

int main() {

🟡 2. Better Approach (C++)

long long factorialBetter(int n, long long prod = 1) {
    if (n <= 1) return prod;
    return factorialBetter(n - 1, prod * n);
}

int main() {
    cout << factorialBetter(5) << endl;
    return 0;
}

using namespace std;

long long factorialOptimal(int n) {
    long long ans = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
        ans *= i;
    }
    return ans;
}

Problem 7

Check Armstrong Number

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

An Armstrong number is a number that is the sum of its own digits each raised to the power of the number of digits.

Example 1:
Input: n = 153
Output: true
Explanation: 1^3 + 5^3 + 3^3 = 1 + 125 + 27 = 153.
Example 2:
Input: n = 370
Output: true
Explanation: 3^3 + 7^3 + 0^3 = 27 + 343 + 0 = 370.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Pehle total digits $k = \lfloor \log_{10}(N) \rfloor + 1$ calculate karo. Phir har digit ka power $k$ nikaal kar sum me add karo. Compare `sum == original`.
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: n = 153 (k = 3)
3^3 = 27
5^3 = 125 → 27 + 125 = 152
1^3 = 1 → 152 + 1 = 153 == 153. Returns true!
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Convert to string, compute pow(digit, length) using floating-point std::pow.
Time: O(log10 N) • Space: O(log10 N)
🟡 Better Approach:
Two passes: pass 1 counts digits; pass 2 computes powers using integer loop.
Time: O(log10 N) • Space: O(1)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Compute digit count via log10, accumulate sum with fast integer exponentiation. O(1) space.
Time: O(log10 N) • Space: O(1)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <cmath>
using namespace std;

bool isArmstrongBrute(int n) {
    string s = to_string(n);
    int k = s.length();
    long long sum = 0;
    for (char c : s) {
        sum += pow(c - '0', k);
    }
    return sum == n;
}

int main() {
    cout << (isArmstrongBrute(153) ? "true" : "false") << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <cmath>
using namespace std;

bool isArmstrongBetter(int n) {
    int k = 0, temp = n;
    while (temp > 0) {
        k++;
        temp /= 10;
    }
    temp = n;
    long long sum = 0;
    while (temp > 0) {
        sum += pow(temp % 10, k);
        temp /= 10;
    }
    return sum == n;
}

int main() {
    cout << (isArmstrongBetter(153) ? "true" : "false") << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

long long intPower(int base, int exp) {
    long long res = 1;
    while (exp > 0) {
        if (exp & 1) res *= base;
        base *= base;
        exp >>= 1;
    }
    return res;
}

bool isArmstrongOptimal(int n) {
    int k = 0, temp = n;
    while (temp > 0) {
        k++;
        temp /= 10;
    }
    temp = n;
    long long sum = 0;
    while (temp > 0) {
        sum += intPower(temp % 10, k);
        if (sum > n) return false;
        temp /= 10;
    }
    return sum == n;
}

int main() {
    cout << (isArmstrongOptimal(153) ? "true" : "false") << endl;
    return 0;
}
Problem 8

Check for Perfect Number

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

A perfect number is a positive integer that is equal to the sum of its positive proper divisors, excluding the number itself.

Example 1:
Input: n = 28
Output: true
Explanation: Divisors of 28 are 1, 2, 4, 7, 14. 1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14 = 28.
Example 2:
Input: n = 6
Output: true
Explanation: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Symmetric Divisor Property: Divisors hamesha pairs me aate hain $(i, N / i)$. Isliye hume sirf $1$ se $\sqrt{N}$ tak iterate karna hai! Time drops from $O(N)$ to $O(\sqrt{N})$!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: n = 28
i = 1: add 1
i = 2: add 2 + (28/2 = 14) = 16
i = 4: add 4 + (28/4 = 7) = 11
Total = 1 + 16 + 11 = 28 == 28. Returns true!
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Iterate from 1 to n - 1 and sum all factors where (n % i == 0).
Time: O(N) • Space: O(1)
🟡 Better Approach:
Iterate up to n / 2 since no divisor can exceed n / 2.
Time: O(N / 2) = O(N) • Space: O(1)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Iterate up to sqrt(n). Add both i and n / i for each factor. O(sqrt(N)) time, O(1) space.
Time: O(sqrt(N)) • Space: O(1)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

bool checkPerfectNumberBrute(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return false;
    int sum = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        if (n % i == 0) sum += i;
    }
    return sum == n;
}

int main() {
    cout << (checkPerfectNumberBrute(28) ? "true" : "false") << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

bool checkPerfectNumberBetter(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return false;
    int sum = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i * i <= n; i++) {
        if (n % i == 0) {
            sum += i;
            if (i != n / i) sum += (n / i);
        }
    }
    return sum == n;
}

int main() {
    cout << (checkPerfectNumberBetter(28) ? "true" : "false") << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

bool checkPerfectNumberOptimal(int num) {
    if (num <= 1) return false;
    int sum = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i * i <= num; i++) {
        if (num % i == 0) {
            sum += i;
            if (i * i != num) sum += num / i;
        }
        if (sum > num) return false;
    }
    return sum == num;
}

int main() {
    cout << (checkPerfectNumberOptimal(28) ? "true" : "false") << endl;
    return 0;
}
Problem 9

Check for Prime Number

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given an integer n, determine if it is a prime number.

Example 1:
Input: n = 11
Output: true
Explanation: 11 has only two factors: 1 and 11.
Example 2:
Input: n = 4
Output: false
Explanation: 4 is divisible by 2.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Agar number composite hai to kam se kam ek factor $\le \sqrt{N}$ hoga. $6k \pm 1$ optimization: 2 aur 3 se check karo, phir sirf $6k \pm 1$ wale numbers se divide karo! $O(\sqrt{N} / 6)$ lightning-fast check.
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: n = 11
sqrt(11) = 3.31
11 % 2 != 0
11 % 3 != 0
No factors <= 3. 11 is Prime!
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Iterate from 2 to n - 1. If any i divides n, return false.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(1)
🟡 Better Approach:
Iterate from 2 up to sqrt(n). If n % i == 0, return false.
Time: O(sqrt(N)) • Space: O(1)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Check 2 and 3, then increment i by 6 checking i and i + 2 up to sqrt(n). O(sqrt(N)/6) time.
Time: O(sqrt(N)) • Space: O(1)

        if (n % i == 0) return false;
    }
    return true;
}

int main() {
    cout << (isPrimeBrute(29) ? "Prime" : "Not Prime") << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

bool isPrimeBetter(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return false;
    for (int i = 2; i * i <= n; i++) {
        if (n % i == 0) return false;
    }

🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

bool isPrimeOptimal(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return false;
    if (n <= 3) return true;
    if (n % 2 == 0 || n % 3 == 0) return false;
    for (int i = 5; i * i <= n; i += 6) {
        if (n % i == 0 || n % (i + 2) == 0) return false;
    }
    return true;
}

Problem 10

Count Primes Till N (Sieve of Eratosthenes)

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Medium

Given an integer n, return the number of prime numbers strictly less than n.

Example 1:
Input: n = 10
Output: 4
Explanation: There are 4 prime numbers less than 10: 2, 3, 5, 7.
Example 2:
Input: n = 2
Output: 0
Explanation: No prime numbers less than 2.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Sieve of Eratosthenes: Har number ko individually check karne ke bajaye, ek boolean table banao aur primes ke saare multiples ($p^2, p^2 + p, p^2 + 2p...$) ko composite mark karte jao. Complexity drops to $O(N \log(\log N))$!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: n = 10
Prime 2 → mark 4, 6, 8
Prime 3 → mark 9
Primes remaining: 2, 3, 5, 7. Count = 4.
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
For every number i from 2 to n - 1, check primality in O(sqrt(i)).
Time: O(N * sqrt(N)) • Space: O(1)
🟡 Better Approach:
Sieve marking all multiples from 2*p up to n.
Time: O(N log N) • Space: O(N)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Optimized Sieve starting multiple cancellation from p*p up to n. O(N log(log N)) time.
Time: O(N log(log N)) • Space: O(N)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

bool isPrimeCheck(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return false;
    for (int i = 2; i * i <= n; i++) if (n % i == 0) return false;
    return true;
}

int countPrimesBrute(int n) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
        if (isPrimeCheck(i)) count++;
    }
    return count;
}

int main() {
    cout << countPrimesBrute(30) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int countPrimesBetter(int n) {
    if (n < 2) return 0;
    vector<bool> isPrime(n + 1, true);
    isPrime[0] = isPrime[1] = false;
    for (int p = 2; p * p <= n; p++) {
        if (isPrime[p]) {
            for (int i = p * p; i <= n; i += p) isPrime[i] = false;
        }
    }
    int count = 0;
    for (int p = 2; p <= n; p++) if (isPrime[p]) count++;
    return count;
}

int main() {
    cout << countPrimesBetter(30) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int countPrimesOptimal(int n) {
    if (n < 2) return 0;
    vector<bool> isPrime(n + 1, true);
    int count = 1;
    for (int i = 3; i <= n; i += 2) {
        if (isPrime[i]) {
            count++;
            if ((long long)i * i <= n) {
                for (int j = i * i; j <= n; j += 2 * i) isPrime[j] = false;
            }
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main() {
    cout << countPrimesOptimal(30) << endl;
    return 0;
}
Problem 11

GCD (Greatest Common Divisor) of Two Numbers

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given two integers a and b, find their Greatest Common Divisor.

Example 1:
Input: a = 52, b = 10
Output: 2
Explanation: 2 is the largest integer that divides both 52 and 10.
Example 2:
Input: a = 20, b = 15
Output: 5
Explanation: 5 divides 20 and 15.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Euclidean Algorithm: $\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, a \bmod b)$. Subtraction se baar-baar minus karne ke bajaye modulo operation numbers ko exponentially shrink kar deta hai in $O(\log(\min(a, b)))$!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: a = 52, b = 10
gcd(52, 10) → gcd(10, 52 % 10 = 2)
gcd(10, 2) → gcd(2, 10 % 2 = 0)
b == 0 → Result = 2.
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Iterate from min(a, b) down to 1. Return first i that divides both.
Time: O(min(a, b)) • Space: O(1)
🟡 Better Approach:
Repeated subtraction Euclidean algorithm: while (a != b) { if (a > b) a -= b; else b -= a; }
Time: O(max(a, b)) • Space: O(1)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Modulo Euclidean algorithm: while (b != 0) { a %= b; swap(a, b); } return a. O(log(min(a, b))) time.
Time: O(log(min(a, b))) • Space: O(1)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int gcdBrute(int a, int b) {
    int ans = 1;
    for (int i = min(a, b); i >= 1; i--) {
        if (a % i == 0 && b % i == 0) {
            ans = i;
            break;
        }
    }
    return ans;
}

int main() {
    cout << gcdBrute(20, 15) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int gcdBetter(int a, int b) {
    while (a > 0 && b > 0) {
        if (a > b) a = a - b;
        else b = b - a;
    }
    return (a == 0) ? b : a;
}

int main() {
    cout << gcdBetter(20, 15) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int gcdOptimal(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int rem = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = rem;
    }
    return a;
}

int main() {
    cout << gcdOptimal(20, 15) << endl;
    return 0;
}
Problem 12

LCM of Two Numbers

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given two integers a and b, find their Least Common Multiple.

Example 1:
Input: a = 4, b = 6
Output: 12
Explanation: 12 is the smallest positive integer divisible by both 4 and 6.
Example 2:
Input: a = 5, b = 10
Output: 10
Explanation: 10 is divisible by 5 and 10.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Math Formula: $a \times b = \gcd(a, b) \times \operatorname{lcm}(a, b)$. Overflow prevention: $\operatorname{lcm}(a, b) = (a / \gcd(a, b)) \times b$. Pehle divide karo, phir multiply!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: a = 4, b = 6
gcd(4, 6) = 2
lcm = (4 / 2) * 6 = 2 * 6 = 12.
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Iterate multiples of max(a, b) checking divisibility by min(a, b).
Time: O(a * b) • Space: O(1)
🟡 Better Approach:
Prime factorization decomposition for both numbers.
Time: O(sqrt(a) + sqrt(b)) • Space: O(log a + log b)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
GCD identity: (a / gcd(a, b)) * b. O(log(min(a, b))) time, O(1) space.
Time: O(log(min(a, b))) • Space: O(1)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

long long lcmBrute(int a, int b) {
    long long m = max(a, b);
    while (true) {
        if (m % a == 0 && m % b == 0) return m;
        m++;
    }
}

int main() {
    cout << lcmBrute(12, 18) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

long long lcmBetter(int a, int b) {
    long long step = max(a, b);
    long long m = step;
    while (m % min(a, b) != 0) {
        m += step;
    }
    return m;
}

int main() {
    cout << lcmBetter(12, 18) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

long long gcdHelper(long long a, long long b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        long long rem = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = rem;
    }
    return a;
}

long long lcmOptimal(long long a, long long b) {
    return (a / gcdHelper(a, b)) * b;
}

int main() {
    cout << lcmOptimal(12, 18) << endl;
    return 0;
}
Problem 13

Print All Divisors of a Number

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given an integer n, return all of its divisors in sorted ascending order.

Example 1:
Input: n = 36
Output: [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36]
Explanation: All 9 positive divisors of 36.
Example 2:
Input: n = 7
Output: [1, 7]
Explanation: 7 is prime with only two divisors.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Divisor pairs $(i, N / i)$: $1$ se $\sqrt{N}$ tak iterate karo. Agar $i$ divides $N$, to $i$ aur $N / i$ dono ko collect karo. Sort karke return karo in $O(\sqrt{N})$!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: n = 12
i = 1: 1 and 12
i = 2: 2 and 6
i = 3: 3 and 4
Sorted: [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12]
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Linear loop from 1 to n checking if (n % i == 0).
Time: O(N) • Space: O(1) auxiliary
🟡 Better Approach:
Iterate up to n / 2, add divisors, append n at end.
Time: O(N / 2) = O(N) • Space: O(1) auxiliary
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Square root loop: iterate up to sqrt(n), push i and n / i. Sort result. O(sqrt(N)) time.
Time: O(sqrt(N)) • Space: O(sqrt(N))
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

void printDivisorsBrute(int n) {
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        if (n % i == 0) cout << i << " ";
    }
    cout << endl;
}

int main() {
    printDivisorsBrute(36);
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

void printDivisorsBetter(int n) {
    vector<int> divs;
    for (int i = 1; i * i <= n; i++) {
        if (n % i == 0) {
            divs.push_back(i);
            if (i != n / i) divs.push_back(n / i);
        }
    }
    sort(divs.begin(), divs.end());
    for (int d : divs) cout << d << " ";
    cout << endl;
}

int main() {
    printDivisorsBetter(36);
    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

void printDivisorsOptimal(int n) {
    vector<int> largeDivs;
    for (int i = 1; i * i <= n; i++) {
        if (n % i == 0) {
            cout << i << " ";
            if (i != n / i) largeDivs.push_back(n / i);
        }
    }
    for (int i = (int)largeDivs.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        cout << largeDivs[i] << " ";
    }
    cout << endl;
}

int main() {
    printDivisorsOptimal(36);
    return 0;
}

1. Introduction: Array Architecture & Memory Layout

Array ek linear data structure hai jisme same data type ke multiple elements contiguous (lagaatar) memory locations par store hote hain. Array DSA ka foundational pillar hai kyunki advanced techniques jaise Two Pointers, Sliding Window, Prefix Sum, aur Binary Search sabhi arrays par hi build hoti hain.

Contiguous Memory Allocation Model: int arr[] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
10
Index 0
0x1000
20
Index 1
0x1004
30
Index 2
0x1008
40
Index 3
0x100C
50
Index 4
0x1010

Random Access Formula: Index i ka memory address directly calculate hota hai: Address = BaseAddress + (i × sizeof(data_type)). Isliye array me index lookup constant time O(1) operation hai.

Interview Best Practice: Pass by Reference (const vector<int>& arr)
  • & (Reference): Poore 105 elements ko memory me dobara copy nahi karta, zero overhead rehta hai.
  • const (Immutable): Function galti se bhi input data ko mutate/modify nahi kar sakta, ensuring bug-free safe code.

2. The 14 Core Array Problems: Brute, Better & Optimal Solutions

Problem 1

Sum of Array Elements

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given an integer array arr of size n, compute and return the sum of all elements.

Example 1:
Input: arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
Output: 15
Explanation: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15.
Example 2:
Input: arr = [10, -2, 5]
Output: 13
Explanation: 10 + (-2) + 5 = 13.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Array ke har element ko bari-bari visit karo aur ek running variable long long sum = 0 me accumulate karo. Standard single loop traversal $O(N)$ time me solve ho jata hai.
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
i = 0: sum = 0 + 1 = 1
i = 1: sum = 1 + 2 = 3
i = 2: sum = 3 + 3 = 6
i = 3: sum = 6 + 4 = 10
i = 4: sum = 10 + 5 = 15
Return 15
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Divide and conquer recursion: sum left half and right half recursively.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(log N) stack
🟡 Better Approach:
Use STL std::accumulate(arr.begin(), arr.end(), 0LL).
Time: O(N) • Space: O(1)
🟢 Optimal Approach:

🟢 Optimal Approach:
Single linear scan: if (arr[i] < arr[i - 1]) return false. Returns true if loop finishes.

Problem 4

Reverse an Array

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given an array arr, reverse the elements in-place using two pointers.

Example 1:
Input: arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
Output: [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
Explanation: First and last elements swapped inward until array is inverted.
Example 2:
Input: arr = [10, 20]
Output: [20, 10]
Explanation: Two elements swapped.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Two Pointers converging inward: left = 0 aur right = n - 1. Har step par swap(arr[left++], arr[right--]) karo jab tak pointers cross na kar jayein. $O(1)$ memory me perfectly in-place!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
left=0, right=4: swap(1, 5) → [5, 2, 3, 4, 1]
left=1, right=3: swap(2, 4) → [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
left=2, right=2: left == right → Terminate. Fully reversed!
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Create auxiliary array of size N, copy elements backwards from original array, then copy back.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(N)
🟡 Better Approach:
Use std::reverse(arr.begin(), arr.end()).
Time: O(N) • Space: O(1)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Two pointers inward swap: while (left < right) swap(arr[left++], arr[right--]). O(1) space.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(1)

Problem 6

Second Largest and Second Smallest in Array

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given an array of integers, find the second largest and second smallest distinct elements without sorting.

Example 1:
Input: arr = [1, 2, 4, 7, 7, 5]
Output: Second Largest: 5, Second Smallest: 2
Explanation: Largest is 7 → second largest is 5. Smallest is 1 → second smallest is 2.
Example 2:
Input: arr = [10, 10, 10]
Output: -1, -1
Explanation: No distinct second elements exist.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Single Pass tracking: largest = INT_MIN, secLargest = INT_MIN. Agar current element arr[i] > largest hai, to purana largest second largest ban jata hai (secLargest = largest; largest = arr[i];). Single loop me bina sorting ke dono mil jate hain!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: arr = [1, 2, 4, 7, 5]
x = 1: largest = 1, sec = -inf
x = 2: sec = 1, largest = 2
x = 4: sec = 2, largest = 4
x = 7: sec = 4, largest = 7
x = 5: 5 < 7 and 5 > 4 → sec = 5, largest = 7
Second Largest = 5
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Sort array ascending. Traverse from end for second distinct largest, and from start for second distinct smallest.
Time: O(N log N) • Space: O(1)
🟡 Better Approach:
Two passes: pass 1 finds largest and smallest; pass 2 finds second largest (< largest) and second smallest (> smallest).
Time: O(2N) = O(N) • Space: O(1)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Single pass: update largest and cascade previous largest to secondLargest. Same logic for smallest and secondSmallest.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(1)

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

pair<int, int> secondOrderBrute(vector<int>& arr) {
    int n = arr.size();
    if (n < 2) return {-1, -1};
    sort(arr.begin(), arr.end());
    int sLargest = -1, sSmallest = -1;
    for (int i = n - 2; i >= 0; i--) {
        if (arr[i] != arr.back()) { sLargest = arr[i]; break; }
    }
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        if (arr[i] != arr[0]) { sSmallest = arr[i]; break; }
    }
    return {sLargest, sSmallest};
}

int main() {
    vector<int> arr = {1, 2, 4, 7, 7, 5};
    auto [sL, sS] = secondOrderBrute(arr);
    cout << sL << " " << sS << endl;
    return 0;
}

pair<int, int> secondOrderBetter(const vector<int>& arr) {

    for (int x : arr) {
        if (x < small) small = x;
        if (x > large) large = x;
    }
    int sSmall = INT_MAX, sLarge = INT_MIN;
    for (int x : arr) {
        if (x > sLarge && x != large) sLarge = x;
        if (x < sSmall && x != small) sSmall = x;
    }
    return {sLarge, sSmall};
}

using namespace std;

pair<int, int> secondOrderOptimal(const vector<int>& arr) {

        if (x > large) { sLarge = large; large = x; }
        else if (x > sLarge && x != large) sLarge = x;
        if (x < small) { sSmall = small; small = x; }
        else if (x < sSmall && x != small) sSmall = x;

}

In-place shift: save temp = arr[0], shift arr[i - 1] = arr[i] from 1 to n-1, set arr[n - 1] = temp. O(1) space.

Problem 8

Left Rotate an Array by K Places

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Medium

Given an array arr, rotate the array to the left by k positions in-place.

Example 1:
Input: arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], k = 3
Output: [4, 5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3]

Output: [3, 99, -1, -100]
Explanation: First 2 elements [-1, -100] move to end.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Reversal Algorithm Trick: k = k % n. (1) First k elements ko reverse karo: reverse(0, k - 1), (2) Remaining elements ko reverse karo: reverse(k, n - 1), (3) Poore array ko reverse karo: reverse(0, n - 1). Zero extra space me $O(N)$ rotation!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 2
Step 1: Reverse first 2 [1, 2] → [2, 1, 3, 4, 5]
Step 2: Reverse remaining 3 [3, 4, 5] → [2, 1, 5, 4, 3]
Step 3: Reverse entire array → [3, 4, 5, 1, 2]
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Rotate array by 1 place k times in a loop.
Time: O(N * K) • Space: O(1)
🟡 Better Approach:
Store first k elements in a temp array, shift remaining elements left, copy temp to end.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(K)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Reversal algorithm: reverse(0, k-1), reverse(k, n-1), reverse(0, n-1). In-place O(1) space.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(1)

void rotateKBrute(vector<int>& arr, int k) {

    while (k--) {
        int temp = arr[0];
        for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) arr[i - 1] = arr[i];
        arr[n - 1] = temp;
    }
}

    for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) arr[n - k + i] = temp[i];

Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given an integer array nums, move all 0's to the end of it while maintaining the relative order of the non-zero elements in-place.

i = 1: nums[1]=1 != 0 → swap(nums[1], nums[0]) → [1, 0, 0, 3, 12], j=1
i = 2: nums[2]=0 → skip
i = 3: nums[3]=3 != 0 → swap(nums[3], nums[1]) → [1, 3, 0, 0, 12], j=2
i = 4: nums[4]=12 != 0 → swap(nums[4], nums[2]) → [1, 3, 12, 0, 0], j=3
Result: [1, 3, 12, 0, 0]
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Copy all non-zero elements to a temp vector, fill remaining with zeroes, copy back.
Time: O(2N) = O(N) • Space: O(N)
🟡 Better Approach:
Overwriting: place non-zero elements at index count++, then fill remaining indices with 0.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(1)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Two pointers swap: find first zero at j; for each non-zero at i, swap(nums[i], nums[j++]). O(N) time, O(1) space.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(1)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

void moveZeroesBrute(vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = nums.size();
    vector<int> temp;
    for (int x : nums) if (x != 0) temp.push_back(x);
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)temp.size(); i++) nums[i] = temp[i];
    for (int i = temp.size(); i < n; i++) nums[i] = 0;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {0, 1, 0, 3, 12};
    moveZeroesBrute(nums);
    for (int x : nums) cout << x << " ";
    cout << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

void moveZeroesBetter(vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = nums.size();
    int pos = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (nums[i] != 0) nums[pos++] = nums[i];
    }
    while (pos < n) nums[pos++] = 0;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {0, 1, 0, 3, 12};
    moveZeroesBetter(nums);
    for (int x : nums) cout << x << " ";
    cout << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <utility>
using namespace std;

void moveZeroesOptimal(vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = nums.size();
    int j = -1;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (nums[i] == 0) { j = i; break; }
    }
    if (j == -1) return;
    for (int i = j + 1; i < n; i++) {
        if (nums[i] != 0) {
            swap(nums[i], nums[j]);
            j++;
        }
    }
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {0, 1, 0, 3, 12};
    moveZeroesOptimal(nums);
    for (int x : nums) cout << x << " ";
    cout << endl;
    return 0;
}
Problem 10

Linear Search in Array

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given an array arr and a target integer target, return the first index of target, or -1 if target is not present.

Example 1:
Input: arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], target = 3
Output: 2
Explanation: 3 is present at index 2.
Example 2:
Input: arr = [5, 4, 3, 2, 1], target = 10
Output: -1
Explanation: 10 is not in the array.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Index 0 se n-1 tak sequence me scan karo. Jaise hi arr[i] == target, index i return kar do. Loop ke baad agar nahi mila to -1 return karo.
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: arr = [10, 20, 30], target = 20
i = 0: 10 != 20
i = 1: 20 == 20 → Return index 1
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Linear loop from 0 to n-1 with sequential equality comparison.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(1)
🟡 Better Approach:
Use STL std::find(arr.begin(), arr.end(), target) with iterator difference.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(1)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Single pass iterative scan: return index on first match, -1 if loop ends. O(N) time, O(1) space.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(1)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++

#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int linearSearchBrute(const vector<int>& arr, int num) {
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)arr.size(); i++) {
        if (arr[i] == num) return i;
    }

}

    vector<int> arr = {6, 7, 8, 4, 1};

🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int linearSearchBetter(const vector<int>& arr, int num) {
    auto it = find(arr.begin(), arr.end(), num);
    if (it != arr.end()) return it - arr.begin();
    return -1;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> arr = {6, 7, 8, 4, 1};
    cout << linearSearchBetter(arr, 4) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int linearSearchOptimal(const vector<int>& arr, int num) {
    int left = 0, right = (int)arr.size() - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        if (arr[left] == num) return left;
        if (arr[right] == num) return right;
        left++;
        right--;
    }
    return -1;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> arr = {6, 7, 8, 4, 1};
    cout << linearSearchOptimal(arr, 4) << endl;

}
Problem 11

Union of Two Sorted Arrays

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Medium

Given two sorted arrays a and b, return an array of their union in sorted order without duplicates.

Example 1:
Input: a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], b = [1, 2, 3, 6, 7]
Output: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
Explanation: Common elements {1, 2, 3} included once, along with unique elements {4, 5, 6, 7}.
Example 2:
Input: a = [2, 2, 3, 4, 5], b = [1, 1, 2, 3, 4]
Output: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
Explanation: Duplicates removed and arrays combined.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Two Pointers Merge Technique: i pointer array a me aur j pointer array b me. Chhota element pick karo aur result me sirf tab push karo jab wo result ke pichle element ke barabar na ho (`unionArr.back() != val`). Duplicate automatically skip ho jate hain!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: a = [1, 2, 3], b = [2, 3, 4]
i=0, j=0: 1 < 2 → push 1, i=1. union = [1]
i=1, j=0: 2 == 2 → push 2, i=2, j=1. union = [1, 2]
i=2, j=1: 3 == 3 → push 3, i=3, j=2. union = [1, 2, 3]
j=2: push 4, j=3. union = [1, 2, 3, 4]
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Insert all elements of both arrays into std::set which maintains sorted order and uniqueness.
Time: O((N + M) log(N + M)) • Space: O(N + M)
🟡 Better Approach:
Use unordered_set then copy to vector and sort.
Time: O((N + M) log(N + M)) • Space: O(N + M)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Two pointers merge: compare a[i] and b[j], push smaller element if not duplicate (union.back() != val). O(N + M) time, O(1) auxiliary.
Time: O(N + M) • Space: O(1) auxiliary

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

vector<int> unionArrayBetter(const vector<int>& arr1, const vector<int>& arr2) {
    unordered_map<int, int> freq;
    for (int x : arr1) freq[x]++;
    for (int x : arr2) freq[x]++;
    vector<int> res;
    for (auto& p : freq) res.push_back(p.first);
    sort(res.begin(), res.end());
    return res;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> a = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, b = {2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6};

    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<int> unionArrayOptimal(const vector<int>& a, const vector<int>& b) {
    int n = a.size(), m = b.size();
    int i = 0, j = 0;
    vector<int> res;
    auto addUnique = [&](int val) {
        if (res.empty() || res.back() != val) res.push_back(val);
    };
    while (i < n && j < m) {
        if (a[i] <= b[j]) { addUnique(a[i]); i++; }
        else { addUnique(b[j]); j++; }
    }
    while (i < n) { addUnique(a[i]); i++; }
    while (j < m) { addUnique(b[j]); j++; }
    return res;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> a = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, b = {2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6};
    auto res = unionArrayOptimal(a, b);
    for (int x : res) cout << x << " ";
    cout << endl;
    return 0;
}
Problem 12

Find Missing Number in Array

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given an array nums containing n distinct numbers in the range [0, n], return the only number in the range that is missing.

Example 1:
Input: nums = [3, 0, 1]
Output: 2
Explanation: n = 3 since there are 3 numbers, range [0, 3]. Missing number is 2.
Example 2:
Input: nums = [0, 1]
Output: 2
Explanation: Range is [0, 2], missing number is 2.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
XOR Trick: $x oplus x = 0$ aur $x oplus 0 = x$. Agar hum 0 se $N$ tak ke saare integers ka XOR karein aur array ke saare elements ka XOR karein, to jo bhi number dono jagah maujood hai wo cancel out hokar 0 ban jayega, aur akela missing number directly mil jayega! Zero integer overflow risk!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: nums = [3, 0, 1], n = 3
XOR all indices 0..3: (0 ^ 1 ^ 2 ^ 3) = 0
XOR all elements: (3 ^ 0 ^ 1) = 2
Combined XOR: 0 ^ 2 = 2. Missing number = 2.
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
For every number i from 0 to n, linearly check if i exists in nums.
Time: O(N^2) • Space: O(1)
🟡 Better Approach:
Math sum formula: expected = n * (n + 1) / 2. Subtract each array element to find missing value.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(1)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
XOR property: xorAll = 0..n ^ nums[0..n-1]. All matched pairs cancel to 0, leaving the missing number without overflow risk.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(1)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int missingNumberBrute(const vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = nums.size();
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
        bool found = false;
        for (int x : nums) {
            if (x == i) { found = true; break; }
        }
        if (!found) return i;
    }
    return -1;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {3, 0, 1};
    cout << missingNumberBrute(nums) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int missingNumberBetter(const vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = nums.size();
    vector<bool> present(n + 1, false);
    for (int x : nums) present[x] = true;
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
        if (!present[i]) return i;
    }
    return -1;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {3, 0, 1};
    cout << missingNumberBetter(nums) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int missingNumberOptimal(const vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = nums.size();
    int xorVal = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        xorVal ^= (i ^ nums[i]);
    }
    xorVal ^= n;
    return xorVal;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {3, 0, 1};
    cout << missingNumberOptimal(nums) << endl;
    return 0;
}
Problem 13

Maximum Consecutive Ones

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given a binary array nums, return the maximum number of consecutive 1's in the array.

Example 1:
Input: nums = [1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1]
Output: 3
Explanation: First two digits and last three digits are consecutive 1s. Maximum is 3.
Example 2:
Input: nums = [1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1]
Output: 2
Explanation: Maximum consecutive 1s is 2.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Running streak counter: `curr` aur `maxOnes`. Jab bhi `nums[i] == 1` ho, `curr++` karo aur `maxOnes = max(maxOnes, curr)` karo. Jaise hi `nums[i] == 0` dikhe, streak toot gayi, isliye `curr = 0` reset kar do!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: nums = [1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1]
1 → curr=1, max=1
1 → curr=2, max=2
0 → curr=0, max=2
1 → curr=1, max=2
1 → curr=2, max=2
1 → curr=3, max=3 (Peak)
Answer: 3
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
For every starting index with 1, scan forward to count consecutive 1s.
Time: O(N^2) • Space: O(1)
🟡 Better Approach:
Find lengths between zero indices using vector of zero positions.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(N)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Single pass: curr = (x == 1) ? curr + 1 : 0; maxOnes = max(maxOnes, curr). O(N) time, O(1) space.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(1)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int findMaxConsecutiveOnesBrute(const vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = nums.size();
    int maxCount = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (nums[i] == 1) {
            int count = 0;
            for (int j = i; j < n && nums[j] == 1; j++) count++;
            maxCount = max(maxCount, count);
        }
    }
    return maxCount;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1};
    cout << findMaxConsecutiveOnesBrute(nums) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int findMaxConsecutiveOnesBetter(const vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = nums.size();
    int maxCount = 0, left = 0;
    for (int right = 0; right < n; right++) {
        if (nums[right] == 0) {
            left = right + 1;
        } else {
            maxCount = max(maxCount, right - left + 1);
        }
    }
    return maxCount;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1};
    cout << findMaxConsecutiveOnesBetter(nums) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int findMaxConsecutiveOnesOptimal(const vector<int>& nums) {
    int maxCount = 0, curr = 0;
    for (int x : nums) {
        if (x == 1) {
            curr++;
            if (curr > maxCount) maxCount = curr;
        } else {
            curr = 0;
        }
    }
    return maxCount;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1};
    cout << findMaxConsecutiveOnesOptimal(nums) << endl;

}
Problem 14

Single Number (Appears Once)

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given a non-empty array of integers nums, every element appears twice except for one. Find that single one in linear time and constant space.

Example 1:
Input: nums = [2, 2, 1]
Output: 1
Explanation: 2 appears twice, 1 appears once.
Example 2:
Input: nums = [4, 1, 2, 1, 2]
Output: 4
Explanation: 1 and 2 appear twice, 4 appears once.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
XOR Bitwise Magic: $x oplus x = 0$ aur $x oplus 0 = x$. Array ke saare elements ka XOR le lo: `ans ^= nums[i]`. Har pair cancel ho kar 0 ho jayega, aur jo akela number ek baar aaya hai wo directly result me nikal aayega!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: nums = [4, 1, 2, 1, 2]
4 ^ 1 ^ 2 ^ 1 ^ 2 = 4 ^ (1 ^ 1) ^ (2 ^ 2) = 4 ^ 0 ^ 0 = 4.
Single unique number: 4
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
For each element, count frequency across the array using a nested loop. Return element with count == 1.
Time: O(N^2) • Space: O(1)
🟡 Better Approach:
Use unordered_map to count frequencies and return key with value 1.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(N)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
XOR accumulation: ans = 0; for (x : nums) ans ^= x; return ans. O(N) time, O(1) space.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(1)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int singleNumberBrute(const vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = nums.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        int count = 0;
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
            if (nums[j] == nums[i]) count++;
        }
        if (count == 1) return nums[i];
    }
    return -1;
}

    vector<int> nums = {4, 1, 2, 1, 2};
    cout << singleNumberBrute(nums) << endl;

Chapter 7 • Hashing Fundamentals & Frequency Maps

DSA Basic Hashing — Complete C++ Notes: Frequency Counting, Extremes & Map Patterns

Brute • Better • Optimal • Hash Tables • std::unordered_map • Frequency Counting

1. Introduction: What is Hashing & Frequency Counting?

Hashing ek fundamental data structuring technique hai jisme hum kisi key ya element ko hash function ke through memory bucket index me convert karke associated values store karte hain. Iska primary advantage hai O(1) average-time search, insertion, aur update.

DSA aur competitive programming me Hashing ka sabse widely used pattern hai Frequency Counting (yaani array me kaunsa element kitni baar appear hua hai). Yeh technique Majority Element, Anagrams, Top K Frequent Elements, aur Subarray Sum Equals K jaise advanced problems ka base banati hai.

Container Internal Data Structure Average Time Complexity Worst Case Time Key Ordering
std::unordered_map<K, V> Hash Table with Chaining/Buckets O(1) O(N) (Hash Collisions) Unordered (Random)
std::map<K, V> Red-Black Self-Balancing BST O(log N) O(log N) (Guaranteed) Sorted by Key (Ascending)
The freq[x]++ Idiom Breakdown:
  1. Agar key x map me pehle se present nahi hai, to C++ automatically use value 0 ke saath insert kar deta hai.
  2. Uske baad ++ operator uski value ko increment karke 1 kar deta hai.
  3. Agar key x pehle se exist karti hai, to existing frequency me simply +1 add ho jata hai.

2. The 6 Core Hashing Problems: Brute, Better & Optimal Solutions

Problem 1

Highest Occurring Element in Array

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given an array of integers nums, find the element that occurs with the highest frequency. If multiple elements have the same maximum frequency, return the smallest element among them.

Example 1:
Input: nums = [1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 2]
Output: 2
Explanation: Element 2 occurs 3 times, which is the highest frequency.
Example 2:
Input: nums = [4, 4, 5, 5, 6]
Output: 4
Explanation: Both 4 and 5 occur 2 times. The smaller element 4 is returned.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Array me har unique element ka count rakhne ke liye unordered_map<int, int> sabse best choice hai. Map banne ke baad ek single pass me max frequency track karo aur tie-breaking condition (element < maxEle) handle karo.
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: nums = [1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 2]
inums[i]Map StateCurrent Max FreqMax Element
01{1: 1}11
12{1: 1, 2: 1}11 (1 < 2)
22{1: 1, 2: 2}22
33{1: 1, 2: 2, 3: 1}22
41{1: 2, 2: 2, 3: 1}21 (1 < 2)
52{1: 2, 2: 3, 3: 1}32
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
For each element, count its occurrences across the array using a nested loop and track the maximum frequency found.
Time: O(N^2) • Space: O(1)
🟡 Better Approach:
Sort array using std::sort. Consecutive identical elements group together; count runs to determine the maximum frequency.
Time: O(N log N) • Space: O(1)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Use an unordered_map to count frequencies in a single pass O(N), then find the key with maximum count and smallest value.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(N)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int highestOccurringBrute(const vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = nums.size();
    int maxFreq = 0;
    int ans = -1;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        int count = 0;
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
            if (nums[j] == nums[i]) count++;
        }
        if (count > maxFreq || (count == maxFreq && nums[i] < ans)) {
            maxFreq = count;
            ans = nums[i];
        }
    }
    return ans;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 2};
    cout << highestOccurringBrute(nums) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int highestOccurringBetter(vector<int> nums) {
    sort(nums.begin(), nums.end());
    int maxFreq = 1, currentFreq = 1;
    int ans = nums[0];
    for (size_t i = 1; i < nums.size(); i++) {
        if (nums[i] == nums[i - 1]) {
            currentFreq++;
        } else {
            if (currentFreq > maxFreq) {
                maxFreq = currentFreq;
                ans = nums[i - 1];
            }
            currentFreq = 1;
        }
    }
    if (currentFreq > maxFreq) ans = nums.back();
    return ans;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {4, 4, 5, 5, 6};
    cout << highestOccurringBetter(nums) << endl;
    return 0;
}

Problem 2

Second Highest Occurring Element in Array

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given an array of integers nums, find the element that has the second highest frequency. If a tie occurs, return the smaller element.

Example 1:
Input: nums = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]
Output: 2
Explanation: Frequencies: 3 appears 3 times (highest), 2 appears 2 times (second highest), 1 appears 1 time.
Example 2:
Input: nums = [1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]
Output: 1
Explanation: Elements 1 and 2 both appear 2 times (second highest). Smaller element 1 is returned.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Pehle pass me map se absolute highest frequency (maxFreq) nikal lo. Doosre pass me aise element ko find karo jiski frequency strictly < maxFreq ho par baaki sabse badi ho!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: nums = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]
Step 1 (Frequency Map): {1: 1, 2: 2, 3: 3}.
Step 2 (Find maxFreq): Max frequency = 3 (element 3).
Step 3 (Find secondMaxFreq < 3): Checking remaining elements: frequency 2 for element 2, frequency 1 for element 1. Second max frequency = 2!
Winner: Element = 2 (Frequency = 2)
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Count frequencies with nested loops, extract unique elements into a list, sort by frequency descending, and pick the second unique frequency.
Time: O(N^2) • Space: O(N)
🟡 Better Approach:
Sort array, compute run-length frequencies into a vector of pairs, sort pairs by frequency, and return the second highest.
Time: O(N log N) • Space: O(N)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Use unordered_map. In pass 1 find maxFreq. In pass 2 track max frequency strictly less than maxFreq with tie-breaker.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(N)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int secondHighestBrute(const vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = nums.size();
    vector<pair<int, int>> freqs;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        bool seen = false;
        for (int k = 0; k < i; k++) {
            if (nums[k] == nums[i]) { seen = true; break; }
        }
        if (seen) continue;
        int count = 0;
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
            if (nums[j] == nums[i]) count++;
        }
        freqs.push_back({count, nums[i]});
    }
    sort(freqs.begin(), freqs.end(), [](const pair<int,int>& a, const pair<int,int>& b) {
        if (a.first != b.first) return a.first > b.first;
        return a.second < b.second;
    });
    int maxF = freqs[0].first;
    for (auto& p : freqs) {
        if (p.first < maxF) return p.second;
    }
    return -1;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3};
    cout << secondHighestBrute(nums) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int secondHighestBetter(vector<int> nums) {
    sort(nums.begin(), nums.end());
    vector<pair<int, int>> freqs;
    int count = 1;
    for (size_t i = 1; i < nums.size(); i++) {
        if (nums[i] == nums[i - 1]) count++;
        else {
            freqs.push_back({count, nums[i - 1]});
            count = 1;
        }
    }
    freqs.push_back({count, nums.back()});
    sort(freqs.begin(), freqs.end(), [](const pair<int,int>& a, const pair<int,int>& b) {
        if (a.first != b.first) return a.first > b.first;
        return a.second < b.second;
    });
    int maxF = freqs[0].first;
    for (auto& p : freqs) {
        if (p.first < maxF) return p.second;
    }
    return -1;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3};
    cout << secondHighestBetter(nums) << endl;

🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <unordered_map>
using namespace std;

int secondHighestOptimal(const vector<int>& nums) {
    unordered_map<int, int> freq;
    for (int x : nums) freq[x]++;
    int maxF = 0;
    for (auto& p : freq) maxF = max(maxF, p.second);
    int secF = 0;
    int ans = -1;
    for (auto& p : freq) {
        if (p.second < maxF) {
            if (p.second > secF || (p.second == secF && p.first < ans)) {
                secF = p.second;
                ans = p.first;
            }
        }
    }
    return ans;
}

Problem 3

Sum of Highest and Lowest Frequency

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given an array, find the sum of the highest occurring frequency and the lowest occurring frequency among all distinct elements in the array.

Example 1:
Input: nums = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]
Output: 4
Explanation: Max frequency = 3 (element 3), Min frequency = 1 (element 1). Sum = 3 + 1 = 4.
Example 2:
Input: nums = [5, 5, 5, 5]
Output: 8
Explanation: Single distinct element 5 has max frequency 4 and min frequency 4. Sum = 4 + 4 = 8.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Bas frequency map bana kar uske values (counts) ko iterate karo. Ek maxFreq = INT_MIN aur ek minFreq = INT_MAX rakho. Single loop me dono extremes mil jaate hain!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: nums = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]
Frequencies: freq[1] = 1, freq[2] = 2, freq[3] = 3.
Extremes Scan: maxFreq = max(1, 2, 3) = 3; minFreq = min(1, 2, 3) = 1.
Sum: 3 + 1 = 4.
Answer: 4
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Count frequency of each element with nested loops, store in a vector, find min and max values, and return their sum.
Time: O(N^2) • Space: O(N)
🟡 Better Approach:
Sort array, compute run-lengths to collect distinct frequencies, sort frequencies, and sum the first and last elements.
Time: O(N log N) • Space: O(N)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Use unordered_map to count frequencies in O(N). Track maxFreq and minFreq in a single pass over map and return maxFreq + minFreq.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(N)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <climits>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int sumHighestLowestBrute(const vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = nums.size();
    vector<int> counts;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        bool seen = false;
        for (int k = 0; k < i; k++) {
            if (nums[k] == nums[i]) { seen = true; break; }
        }
        if (seen) continue;
        int count = 0;
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
            if (nums[j] == nums[i]) count++;
        }
        counts.push_back(count);
    }
    int maxF = INT_MIN, minF = INT_MAX;
    for (int c : counts) {
        maxF = max(maxF, c);
        minF = min(minF, c);
    }
    return maxF + minF;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3};
    cout << sumHighestLowestBrute(nums) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++)

    for (size_t i = 1; i < nums.size(); i++) {
        if (nums[i] == nums[i - 1]) count++;
        else {
            counts.push_back(count);
            count = 1;
        }
    }

Problem 4

Character Hashing (Frequency of Characters in String)

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Easy

Given a string s consisting of lowercase English letters, answer queries asking for the frequency of a given character c in $O(1)$ query time.

Example 1:
Input: s = "abcdabefc", query = 'a'
Output: 2
Explanation: Character 'a' appears 2 times at index 0 and index 4.
Example 2:
Input: s = "antigravity", query = 't'
Output: 2
Explanation: Character 't' appears 2 times in the word "antigravity".
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Lowercase English letters sirf 26 hote hain ('a' se 'z'). Hum ek size-26 ka integer array hash[26] = {0} banate hain aur character c ko index c - 'a' par map kar dete hain. Zero map overhead, instant direct memory access!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: s = "aba", query = 'a'
Precomputation on "aba":
• i = 0, char = 'a': hash['a' - 'a'] = hash[0]++ → hash[0] = 1
• i = 1, char = 'b': hash['b' - 'a'] = hash[1]++ → hash[1] = 1
• i = 2, char = 'a': hash['a' - 'a'] = hash[0]++ → hash[0] = 2
Query 'a': Direct array lookup hash['a' - 'a'] returns 2 in $O(1)$ time!
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
For every query character, linearly traverse the entire string from index 0 to N-1 and count matching characters.
Time: O(Q * N) • Space: O(1)
🟡 Better Approach:
Use std::map for balanced BST character hashing with O(log 26) lookup per query.
Time: O(N log 26 + Q log 26) • Space: O(26) = O(1)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Fixed-size frequency array of 26 integers. Map character c to index c - 'a'. Precomputation in O(N), every query answered in O(1).
Time: O(N + Q) • Space: O(1) auxiliary
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

int charFrequencyBrute(const string& s, char query) {
    int count = 0;
    for (char c : s) {
        if (c == query) count++;
    }
    return count;
}

int main() {
    string s = "abcdabefc";
    cout << charFrequencyBrute(s, 'a') << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <map>
using namespace std;

int charFrequencyBetter(const string& s, char query) {
    map<char, int> mp;
    for (char c : s) mp[c]++;
    return mp[query];
}

int main() {
    string s = "antigravity";
    cout << charFrequencyBetter(s, 't') << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int charFrequencyOptimal(const string& s, char query) {
    vector<int> hash(26, 0);
    for (char c : s) hash[c - 'a']++;
    return hash[query - 'a'];
}

int main() {
    string s = "abcdabefc";
    cout << charFrequencyOptimal(s, 'a') << endl;
    return 0;
}
Problem 5

Longest Subarray with Sum K

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Medium

Given an array of integers nums and an integer k, find the length of the longest contiguous subarray that sums to k.

Example 1:
Input: nums = [10, 5, 2, 7, 1, 9], k = 15
Output: 4
Explanation: Subarray [5, 2, 7, 1] sums to 5 + 2 + 7 + 1 = 15, length = 4.
Example 2:
Input: nums = [-1, 2, 3], k = 6
Output: 0
Explanation: No contiguous subarray sums to 6.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Prefix Sum Hashing Formula: Agar index i tak running sum prefixSum hai, to hume pehle ka aisa prefix chahiye jiska sum prefixSum - k ho. Agar map me prefixSum - k index j par milta hai, to subarray (j..i] ka sum exactly $k$ hoga aur length $i - j$ hogi!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: nums = [10, 5, 2, 7, 1, 9], k = 15
inums[i]sumsum == k?need (sum - k) in map?maxLen
01010Noneed -5 → No, store mp[10]=00
1515Yessum == 15 → len = 1 + 1 = 22
2217Noneed 2 → No, store mp[17]=22
3724Noneed 9 → No, store mp[24]=32
4125Noneed 10 → Found at index 0! (4 - 0 = 4)4
5934Noneed 19 → No4
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Check all subarrays using two nested loops (i, j). Maintain running sum and update maximum length whenever sum == k.
Time: O(N^2) • Space: O(1)
🟡 Better Approach:
Prefix sum array combined with linear scan for subarray matches.
Time: O(N^2) • Space: O(N)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Prefix sum with unordered_map storing first occurrence index of each prefix sum. If (prefixSum - k) exists in map, update maxLen = max(maxLen, i - map[prefixSum - k]).
Time: O(N) • Space: O(N)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int longestSubarraySumKBrute(const vector<int>& nums, int k) {
    int n = nums.size();
    int maxLen = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        long long sum = 0;
        for (int j = i; j < n; j++) {
            sum += nums[j];
            if (sum == k) {
                maxLen = max(maxLen, j - i + 1);
            }
        }
    }
    return maxLen;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {10, 5, 2, 7, 1, 9};
    cout << longestSubarraySumKBrute(nums, 15) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int longestSubarraySumKBetter(const vector<int>& nums, int k) {
    int n = nums.size();
    vector<long long> pref(n + 1, 0);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) pref[i + 1] = pref[i] + nums[i];
    int maxLen = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        for (int j = i; j < n; j++) {
            if (pref[j + 1] - pref[i] == k) {
                maxLen = max(maxLen, j - i + 1);
            }
        }
    }
    return maxLen;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {10, 5, 2, 7, 1, 9};
    cout << longestSubarraySumKBetter(nums, 15) << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int longestSubarraySumKOptimal(const vector<int>& nums, int k) {
    unordered_map<long long, int> prefixMap;
    long long sum = 0;
    int maxLen = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)nums.size(); i++) {
        sum += nums[i];
        if (sum == k) {
            maxLen = i + 1;
        }
        long long rem = sum - k;
        if (prefixMap.find(rem) != prefixMap.end()) {
            maxLen = max(maxLen, i - prefixMap[rem]);
        }
        if (prefixMap.find(sum) == prefixMap.end()) {
            prefixMap[sum] = i;
        }
    }
    return maxLen;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {10, 5, 2, 7, 1, 9};
    cout << longestSubarraySumKOptimal(nums, 15) << endl;
    return 0;
}
Problem 6

Top K Frequent Elements

Brute • Better • Optimal
Problem Statement Difficulty: Medium

Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. You may return the answer in any order.

Example 1:
Input: nums = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], k = 2
Output: [1, 2]
Explanation: 1 occurs 3 times and 2 occurs 2 times. The 2 most frequent elements are [1, 2].
Example 2:
Input: nums = [1], k = 1
Output: [1]
Explanation: Only 1 element in array with frequency 1.
💡 Core Intuition / Kaise Sochen:
Array me kisi bhi element ki maximum frequency N se badi nahi ho sakti. Isliye hum Bucket Sort use kar sakte hain! buckets[N + 1] array banate hain jahan bucket index frequency ko represent karta hai. Peechhe se scan karke $O(N)$ me bina sorting ke top $k$ elements nikal aate hain!
🔍 Step-by-Step Dry Run (Optimal Approach) Sample: nums = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], k = 2
Step 1 (Frequency Map): {1: 3, 2: 2, 3: 1}.
Step 2 (Bucket by Frequency):
• bucket[1] = [3]
• bucket[2] = [2]
• bucket[3] = [1]
Step 3 (Right-to-Left Scan):
• bucket[3] has 1 → ans = [1]
• bucket[2] has 2 → ans = [1, 2] (size == k = 2 → Exit!)
Final Output: [1, 2]
🔴 Brute Force Approach:
Count frequencies into map, copy all pairs into a vector, sort vector by frequency descending using std::sort, and pick top k.
Time: O(N log N) • Space: O(N)
🟡 Better Approach:
Use a Min-Heap of size k (priority_queue). Keep only top k frequent elements in heap during traversal.
Time: O(N log K) • Space: O(N + K)
🟢 Optimal Approach:
Bucket sort approach: create array of buckets indexed by frequency (from 0 to N). Traverse buckets from N down to 0 collecting elements until k are collected.
Time: O(N) • Space: O(N)
Clean Standard • Zero Comments C++
🔴 1. Brute Force (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

vector<int> topKFrequentBrute(const vector<int>& nums, int k) {
    unordered_map<int, int> freq;
    for (int x : nums) freq[x]++;
    vector<pair<int, int>> arr(freq.begin(), freq.end());
    sort(arr.begin(), arr.end(), [](const pair<int,int>& a, const pair<int,int>& b) {
        return a.second > b.second;
    });
    vector<int> ans;
    for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) ans.push_back(arr[i].first);
    return ans;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3};
    auto res = topKFrequentBrute(nums, 2);
    for (int x : res) cout << x << " ";
    cout << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟡 2. Better Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <queue>
using namespace std;

vector<int> topKFrequentBetter(const vector<int>& nums, int k) {
    unordered_map<int, int> freq;
    for (int x : nums) freq[x]++;
    priority_queue<pair<int,int>, vector<pair<int,int>>, greater<pair<int,int>>> minHeap;
    for (auto& p : freq) {
        minHeap.push({p.second, p.first});
        if ((int)minHeap.size() > k) minHeap.pop();
    }
    vector<int> ans;
    while (!minHeap.empty()) {
        ans.push_back(minHeap.top().second);
        minHeap.pop();
    }
    return ans;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3};
    auto res = topKFrequentBetter(nums, 2);
    for (int x : res) cout << x << " ";
    cout << endl;
    return 0;
}
🟢 3. Optimal Approach (C++) 
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <unordered_map>
using namespace std;

vector<int> topKFrequentOptimal(const vector<int>& nums, int k) {
    int n = nums.size();
    unordered_map<int, int> freq;
    for (int x : nums) freq[x]++;
    vector<vector<int>> buckets(n + 1);
    for (auto& p : freq) buckets[p.second].push_back(p.first);
    vector<int> ans;
    for (int i = n; i >= 0 && (int)ans.size() < k; i--) {
        for (int num : buckets[i]) {
            ans.push_back(num);
            if ((int)ans.size() == k) break;
        }
    }
    return ans;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> nums = {1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3};
    auto res = topKFrequentOptimal(nums, 2);
    for (int x : res) cout << x << " ";
    cout << endl;
    return 0;
}
